question.problem:
Consider the set $B,$ defined as

$$
B=\{\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+1}:n\in \{0,1,2,3,4\}\}.
$$

What is the infimum of $B?$

$inf(B)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The infimum of a set $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B.$

If $B$ is a finite set, the infimum of $B$ equals its minimum.

First, let's write down all the terms of our set by substituting $n=0,1,2,3,4$ into the expression for the elements of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(0)^{2}+1} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{(1)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{(2)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{1}{(3)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{(4)^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{17}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
B=\{1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{5},\,\frac{1}{10},\,\frac{1}{17}\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}inf(B) & =min\{1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{5},\,\frac{1}{10},\,\frac{1}{17}\}=\frac{1}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$
